# Lab 3 — Secure Git: Signed Commits, Secret Scanning, and History Hygiene

## Task 1 — SSH commit signing

Git was configured to sign commits with an SSH key. The relevant signing configuration values are:

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| `gpg.format` | `ssh` |
| `user.signingkey` | `/home/lima.guest/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` |
| `commit.gpgsign` | `true` |

**Evidence — Git signing configuration.**

<img alt="Task 1 evidence showing Git signing configuration values." src="data:image/png;base64," />

A signed test commit was created and verified locally with `git log --show-signature -1`.

```text
commit 159338bc4ac3c3d6ae74a33ce699d4376076c39a
Good "git" signature for 77242035+rmcavalcante7@users.noreply.github.com with ED25519 key SHA256:[redacted fingerprint]
Author:     rmcavalcante7 <77242035+rmcavalcante7@users.noreply.github.com>
AuthorDate: Tue Sep 29 12:32:31 2026 +0000
Commit:     rmcavalcante7 <77242035+rmcavalcante7@users.noreply.github.com>
CommitDate: Tue Sep 29 12:32:31 2026 +0000

    test: first signed commit
```

**Evidence — local signature verification.**

<img alt="Task 1 evidence showing git log --show-signature output for the signed commit." src="data:image/png;base64," />

GitHub also verified the commit signature. The commit is available at:

https://github.com/rmcavalcante7/DevSecOps-Intro/commit/159338bc4ac3c3d6ae74a33ce699d4376076c39a

The GitHub API reported `verified: true` and `reason: valid` for this commit signature.

**Evidence — GitHub Verified commit.**

<img alt="Task 1 evidence showing the signed commit verification on GitHub." src="data:image/png;base64," />

Without commit signing, someone with access to the repository could forge my name and email in the Git author field, making a commit appear to have been created by me. The Verified badge shows that the commit was cryptographically signed with the private key corresponding to the signing key registered with my GitHub account, providing stronger evidence of its origin and reducing the repudiation risk.

## Task 2 — Pre-commit and gitleaks

The repository was configured with `pre-commit` to run secret-scanning and basic safety checks before a commit is created. The configuration uses Gitleaks at a real 8.x tag and two hooks from `pre-commit-hooks`.

```yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.30.1
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks

  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    rev: v6.0.0
    hooks:
      - id: detect-private-key
        exclude: ^labs/lab6/vulnerable-iac/ansible/configure\.yml$
      - id: check-added-large-files
```

**Evidence — pre-commit hook test.**

<img alt="Task 2 evidence showing the pre-commit hook test output." src="data:image/png;base64," />

To test the secret-scanning control, a fake GitHub Personal Access Token was added to `submissions/leak-attempt.txt` and a commit was attempted. The commit was blocked by the Gitleaks hook, which identified the secret as `RuleID: github-pat`.

Relevant blocked-commit output:

```text
Detect hardcoded secrets.................................................Failed
- hook id: gitleaks
- exit code: 1

Finding:     GH_PAT=REDACTED
Secret:      REDACTED
RuleID:      github-pat
File:        submissions/leak-attempt.txt
Line:        1
Fingerprint: submissions/leak-attempt.txt:github-pat:1

WRN leaks found: 1
```

**Evidence — blocked commit attempt.**

<img alt="Task 2 evidence showing the fake GitHub token commit blocked by gitleaks." src="data:image/png;base64," />

The commit did not enter Git history. The latest commit remained the previous signed commit:

```text
159338b test: first signed commit
```

**Evidence — latest commit unchanged after the blocked attempt.**

<img alt="Task 2 evidence showing git log still points to the previous commit after the blocked attempt." src="data:image/png;base64," />

An `[allowlist]` entry in `.gitleaks.toml` can be used to ignore a specific known-safe example, such as a fake `AKIA...` value used in documentation. It stops being safe when the rule is broad enough to also match real credentials, because Gitleaks would no longer report them.

Excluding the entire `docs/` path prevents Gitleaks from scanning any file under that directory. This becomes unsafe if a real secret is accidentally or intentionally added there, because the whole directory is outside the secret-scanning protection.

## Bonus — Purge a secret from history

A disposable sandbox repository was created under `/tmp/lab3-bonus` for the history rewrite exercise. The real course repository was not rewritten.

Before rewriting the sandbox history, the commit log was:

```text
0c09f19 docs: usage notes
5aba195 feat: empty log
68e7132 feat: add config
501361c init
```

After rewriting the history with `git filter-repo`, the commit log became:

```text
dbb4ffa docs: usage notes
308e21e feat: empty log
50a7913 feat: add config
6608deb init
```

The commit hashes changed because Git commits include references to their parent commits. Once an earlier commit was rewritten, the following commits also received new hashes.

The required grep counts were:

```text
Before rewrite:
git log -p | grep -c 'ghp_AAAA'
2

After rewrite:
git log -p | grep -c 'ghp_AAAA'
0

After rewrite:
git log -p | grep -c 'REDACTED'
2
```

This shows that the two occurrences of the fake secret were removed from the rewritten history and replaced with `[REDACTED]`.

On the first attempt, `git filter-repo` refused to rewrite the repository:

```text
Aborting: Refusing to destructively overwrite repo history since
this does not look like a fresh clone.
(expected at most one entry in the reflog for HEAD)
Please operate on a fresh clone instead. If you want to proceed
anyway, use --force.
```

Because the repository was a disposable sandbox created specifically for this exercise, the rewrite was rerun with `--force`:

```text
git filter-repo --replace-text /tmp/replace.txt --force
```

Rewriting Git history is not enough to end a real secret-leak incident. The exposed credential must also be revoked or rotated, because someone may already have copied it before it was removed from the repository.

Two things were surprising. First, `git filter-repo` refused to run even though the sandbox repository had just been created, because it considered the reflog state unsafe for rewriting without explicit confirmation. Second, commit hashes changed after the rewrite, including commits that did not directly contain the secret, because each Git commit depends on the hash of its parent commit.

**Evidence — history rewrite and grep counts.**

<img alt="Bonus evidence showing git-filter-repo history rewrite, grep counts, refusal message, and redacted secret counts." src="data:image/png;base64," />
